subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a weekly application routine [Action]
passage: I'm Madhav, and my job search only started working when it turned into small tasks. Before, I would sit down on Sunday thinking apply everywhere, and freeze. Now I have a weekly quota in a spreadsheet: eight custom applications, two messages asking alumni for referrals, and one practice interview. Monday and Tuesday, three applications each. Wednesday, the referral messages. Thursday evening, a mock interview with Afreen, who asks tough questions and then gives honest feedback. Friday, the last two applications. Each row turns green when it's done. Some weeks I hit seven of eight, and that's fine. Looking back, what changed was that get a job stopped being one huge thing and became small ticks I could finish in a day.

qa.a: The weekly quota is eight custom applications, two messages asking alumni for referrals and one practice interview.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel about the search before the routine?
qa.a: Madhav felt frozen and overwhelmed when thinking apply everywhere.

qa.q: What could Madhav adjust if the applications get no replies?
qa.a: Madhav could ask Afreen or alumni to review a few applications and adjust the resume, since the routine shows where to change.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the mock interviews?
qa.a: Afreen probably feels useful, since Afreen asks tough questions and gives feedback that helps Madhav.

grounding: A student sets a weekly quota of tailored applications, referral messages and a mock interview, tracked in a spreadsheet, so the search becomes small tasks.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a weekly application routine [Action]
passage:
Placement mentor's note, week 3 check-in with Kavitha.
When Kavitha first came to me she had a tab open for every company she'd heard of and had sent nothing in ten days. "It's too big," she said. We broke it down together: each week, eight applications tailored to the posting, two messages asking alumni for referrals, and one mock interview with her classmate Gurleen. She built a spreadsheet with a row for each application: company, date, which resume version, reply.
Today's sheet shows 24 applications over three weeks, six referral messages and three mocks. Two companies have replied, one with a test. More importantly, she told me she now sits down each morning knowing exactly what enough looks like for the day.
What I'll do next: review two of her tailored resumes before Friday, and put her in touch with an alumna who works at the company that sent the test.

qa.q: How many applications does the sheet show after three weeks?
How did Kavitha feel before the plan?
qa.a: Kavitha felt overwhelmed, saying it was too big and sending nothing in ten days.

qa.q: What else could keep Kavitha's routine working?
qa.a: She could add a weekly look at which resume versions get replies, so the eight applications improve over time.

qa.q: How might Gurleen be affected by the weekly mock interviews?
qa.a: Gurleen gets regular practice too, since playing interviewer shows what strong and weak answers sound like.

grounding: Shows a student turning the job search into a weekly quota of eight tailored applications, two referral messages and one mock interview, tracked in a spreadsheet.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a weekly application routine [Action]
passage:
Friday, 10 pm
Week one of the new system, done.
Last month I was "job hunting" every day and had nothing to show for it. Disha said, "You don't need more hours. You need a number." So on Sunday I made a sheet: 8 tailored applications, 2 referral messages, 1 mock interview per week. Every row has the date, the company and what I changed in my resume for them.
Monday and Tuesday: 2 applications each. Wednesday: messaged two seniors, and one already replied. Thursday: 2 more applications. Today: 2 more, and a mock with Disha on a video call. She asked about my final-year project and I rambled for four minutes. Noted.
8 / 2 / 1. All green. First time in weeks I feel like I'm doing the search instead of the search doing me.
Imran

qa.q: How many applications did Imran send on Monday and on Tuesday?
How does Imran feel at the end of week one?
qa.a: Imran feels relieved and more in control, with all three targets green for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What should Imran work on next week?
qa.a: Imran could prepare a short, clear summary of the final-year project, since the mock showed a four-minute ramble.

qa.q: How might Disha see Imran's new system?
qa.a: Disha, who suggested having a number, would likely be pleased that the targets were met and that the mock caught the rambling.

grounding: Illustrates a student breaking the job search into a weekly quota of applications, referral messages and a mock interview tracked in a sheet.
